newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan secures capital to stop Islamist protest.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan secures capital to stop Islamist protest.

text.p: Pakistani authorities diverted trains and blocked roads into the capital, Islamabad, on Saturday to foil a planned anti-corruption protest by Islamic militants, officials and witnesses said.
Qazi Hussain Ahmad, leader of the opposition Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party, denounced Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's government for attributing violent intentions to his followers.
"The rulers have been considering the country their personal property," he said in a statement. "Present state policies have made the life of common lot miserable."
He said his party had never been lawless and urged his supporters to show restraint. The government would be responsible for any "brutal use of force against peaceful protesters," he warned.
The special security measures in Islamabad were designed to block Jamaat-i-Islami's plans to bring a million people to join a sit-in outside parliament.

Officials of state-run Pakistan Railways in the Punjab provincial capital of Lahore said 24 mail and passenger trains that normally pass through Rawalpindi, near Islamabad, had been diverted, suspended or cancelled. Reimbursing passengers would cost an estimated 15 million rupees ($373,000), they said.

Security forces used cranes to block the main road from Lahore to Islamabad with empty containers, witnesses said. The obstacles, on the outskirts of the capital, cut the normal route to the international airport serving Islamabad and Rawalpindi.
Paramilitary forces were earlier drafted into the capital, replacing police who normally guard foreign missions.
In another sign of tension, Islamabad's International School, mainly for American and other foreign children, said it would stay closed on Sunday as a precaution.
Jamaat-i-islami leaders said security forces had rounded up more than 5,500 of its supporters to try to disrupt the planned sit-in.
An Interior Ministry spokesman said this figure was exaggerated, but could not say how many people had been seized. He denied that the party's leader was being sought.
"All this fuss is a smokescreen designed to hide what they know will be a failed event," he said.

Three Jamaat-i-Islami members of parliament resigned their seats in the National Assembly (lower house) on Saturday, following the example of Ahmad, who quit last month to try to put pressure on Bhutto's three-year-old government to resign.
Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar offered on Thursday to release all Jamaat-i-Islami detainees if the party agreed to shift the venue of its sit-in to a park in Rawalpindi.

The party rejected the offer as well as a suggestion by President Farooq Leghari to hold sit-in in Islamabad, but not at parliament, which is close to the presidential palace, prime minister's house, government offices and diplomatic enclave.
Three people were killed and 60 wounded when gunfire broke out during a demonstration by the party in Rawalpindi in June.

The security clampdown coincided with a general strike called by opposition parties and business groups angered by tough new economic measures to persuade the International Monetary Fund to resume a stalled $600 million standby loan.

Witnesses said the stoppage proved partly effective. Some markets and businesses were closed, but there was only limited disruption to transport and many shops and factories stayed open in cities across the country.
